task: Eres concejal de una ciudad turística. Escribe una propuesta de 130–160 palabras con dos medidas contra el exceso de turismo, explicando sus ventajas y un posible inconveniente.
paragraphs: Every summer, the same images appear in the news: narrow streets so crowded that residents cannot reach their front doors, cruise ships towering over historic squares, and locals holding banners that say "Tourists go home". The word for this phenomenon, "overtourism", has entered dictionaries in the last few years.

Tourism is a vital source of income for many places. It creates jobs, keeps restaurants and museums alive and helps to pay for the conservation of monuments. The problem arises when the number of visitors grows faster than the ability of a place to cope with them.

Cheap flights, huge cruise ships and social media have all contributed. A single viral photo can transform a quiet village into a must-see destination overnight. Short-term rental platforms have also changed city centres: when flats are rented to tourists rather than to residents, rents rise, local shops are replaced by souvenir stores, and neighbourhoods slowly lose their character.

Cities are experimenting with different solutions. Venice has introduced a fee for day-trippers on the busiest days. Amsterdam launched a campaign telling certain groups of young visitors to stay away, and several cities have limited the number of tourist flats or banned large cruise ships from their historic centres. Some destinations encourage visitors to come outside the peak season or to explore less famous areas.

Critics of these measures point out that they can turn travel into a privilege for the wealthy and that many workers depend on tourists for their livelihood. Others argue that the measures do not go far enough, since visitor numbers keep breaking records.

Travellers themselves can make a difference, too. Staying longer in one place, travelling out of season, choosing locally owned accommodation and respecting the rules of the places they visit are small decisions, but multiplied by millions of people, they could help ensure that the places we love are still worth visiting in the future.
